When you are spoilt for choice, you have so many good options available that choosing just one becomes genuinely difficult. The "problem" you face is not a lack of good things — it is an abundance of them. Every option looks appealing, and that is exactly what makes the decision hard.

The word "spoilt" here works the same way as in "a spoilt child" — meaning someone who has been given so much that they are overindulged. Apply that idea to options: you have been given so many choices, you are practically overindulged with them. That overindulgence is what "spoilt" captures.

So the phrase carries a gentle irony: the very thing that makes choosing hard is having too much of something good.
The tone and feeling it carries

This is important: being spoilt for choice is not a complaint in the serious sense. It is what people sometimes call a "good problem to have." There is a pleasant, almost grateful undertone to it, even when said with a little sigh of overwhelm.

For example, if a friend says "I'm spoilt for choice" while staring at a menu full of dishes she wants to try, she is not unhappy — she is delightfully overwhelmed.

The options must be desirable. You would not use this phrase if all your choices were equally bad or mediocre. The phrase only makes sense when you genuinely want more than one of the available things — that is the whole source of the difficulty.

"Spoilt for choice" is a predicate adjective, which means it comes after a verb (almost always a form of be), not directly before a noun.

Correct:

"We were spoilt for choice."
"She is absolutely spoilt for choice."

You would not normally say "a spoilt-for-choice situation" in everyday speech, though you might occasionally see it hyphenated in headlines or informal writing.

"With four job offers on the table, Priya was spoilt for choice."

→ She had so many good job options that deciding which to accept was hard — a happy dilemma.

"The bookshop had three floors of fiction alone. I was completely spoilt for choice."

→ Too many appealing books to pick from; the abundance itself was the challenge.

"Our city has excellent metro lines, buses, and auto-rickshaws — commuters are spoilt for choice."

→ So many convenient transport options that any commuter can find something that suits them.

"There were six flavours of ice cream, all homemade. The children were spoilt for choice."

→ Every flavour looked good, making the choice almost paralysing — in a fun way.
What makes this different from just saying "many options"?

Simply saying "there are many options" is neutral — those options might be good, bad, or indifferent. Spoilt for choice tells you two things at once: the options are genuinely good, and the sheer number of them is what creates the difficulty. It is richer and more expressive than "many choices."

This phrase is standard in British, Australian, and Indian English. In American English, "spoiled" is the usual spelling, and while Americans understand the phrase, they are slightly less likely to use it naturally in speech. If you are speaking or writing for a global audience, the phrase is universally understood.

It suits everyday conversation, journalism, reviews, and semi-formal writing equally well. It is not slang, but it is not stiff or academic either.
One-line summary to lock it in
Spoilt for choice = having so many good options that it is hard to pick just one — a difficulty that comes from abundance, not from shortage.
